chapter.title: Writing
chapter.simpara: Project documents use British typography with American phrasing.

listitem.simpara: First-level quotations use single quotes; second-level quotations use double quotes.
Use em dashes (—) for parenthetical content, not en dashes (–).
Use the Oxford comma in lists of three or more items.

chapter.simpara: Every document opens with a short quote in its original language, given only in the original and left untranslated by design — the inaccessibility is intentional, prompting readers to attempt the translation themselves. A document's own epigraph is always in Chinese; from there, each top-level section alternates language, starting with Japanese. Articles carry one such epigraph at the document level and one on each top-level section. Books carry one on each chapter (always Chinese) and one on each top-level section directly under a chapter (alternating from Japanese), but not on the book, preface, or part. Narratives do not carry epigraphs.

Quoted texts are not restricted to the classical era: any Chinese or Japanese text, of any period, is eligible. Texts originally written in another language may also be quoted, but only in Chinese or Japanese translation, and the translation itself must have its own bibliography entry, distinct from any entry for the original work.

A quoted source must have a bibliography entry in shared/bibliography/, referenced from the epigraph's attribution with a personname followed by a citation. Chinese epigraphs use xml:lang="lzh-Hant" for Classical/Literary Chinese; modern Chinese uses xml:lang="zh-Hant" or xml:lang="zh-Hans" according to the script of the source material — a quote from a Simplified-script source keeps its Simplified characters rather than being converted to Traditional. Japanese epigraphs use xml:lang="ja" regardless of period or register.
Bibliography entry files, and their xml:id, are named identically, using a scheme based on the kind of source:

listitem.simpara: Classical or epigraph sources, kept under ja/ or zh/, use a romanised transliteration of the title — pinyin with tone numbers for Chinese, rōmaji for Japanese — since authorship for such sources is often anonymous, pseudepigraphic, or disputed.
Individually authored modern sources use surname-year for one author, surname1-surname2-year for two, or surname1-et-al-year for three or more, all lowercase and hyphenated.
Organisational sources use orgabbreviation-year when the organisation has a recognised abbreviation, or orgname-year otherwise.
A disambiguating a, b, or c suffix is appended only once an actual collision occurs between two entries that would otherwise share the same identifier, never reserved in advance.

chapter.simpara: When a source is nested inside a larger work, biblioset's relation attribute names only an actual DocBook container element — article, book, chapter, or set — never an invented value such as journal or series. The finer bibliographic genre goes on role instead, for example role="essay", role="collection", or role="series".

Between book and set, the deciding question is whether the container is a single physical or material unit. A bounded volume — even one gathering many pieces, such as an author's collected works — is a book. Several volumes cited as one work, as a multi-volume monograph would be, is a set with role="multi-volume". An open-ended series of independently titled books under a shared imprint is a set with role="series".
